subject: Procrustes ANOVA with nested measurement error

messages.author: b35f414539b34a6c
messages.subject: Procrustes ANOVA with nested measurement error
parts:
all,

So I'm struggling to work out how to write the formula for my Procrustes ANOVA in R. I have photographs of 86 human faces, where i took 2 photos each with 2 cameras (4 photos each) and digitised each face twice. I do this because i suspect one camera is more distorted to the other and want to model this distortion, as well as how it possibly interacts with other variables (e.g. fluctuating and directional asymmetry) and sources of measurement error. having 2 digitisations per picture allows me to estimate digitisation error, and 2 pictures allow me to estimate error associated with any 2 pictures (taken 1 minute apart).



So my data is completely nested: digitisations nested in pictures which are nested in camera-type which is nested in individuals. How would i represent this in a procrustes anova formula? I've heard that it's represented as an interaction effect, such that the main effect of digitsation error would be:

individual*camera*picture*digitsation

? 

This terminology would be a problem if i wanted to see if different cameras produce different levels of digitisation error, which I do, as this would be an interaction between the term above and camera, so:

individual*camera*picture*digitisation:camera

Which really doesn't look right.

Really what im trying to get is the main effect of each of my sources of measurement error, as well as 2 way interactions between them and camera type 

Can anyone help me out?

Thanks

Richie

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA with nested measurement error
parts:
Hi Richie,

You will forgive me for answering with a bias toward our functions, but that is the easiest way for me to approach this.

Once you have performed GPA and acquired your Procrustes residuals, call this array, “shape”, you probably want to do an analysis like this:

fit <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind/camera + camera/picture, ...)

Note that “digitization” is not needed as a variable, as it is the error term for picture.  This formula includes ind:camera and camera:picture interactions, but does not assume all levels of one are represented with all levels of the other, in case that is an issue.  (It also does not force the random effect to be represented as a fixed effect in the model.)

For evaluation, you will want to also do this:

fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ camera/picture)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ ind/camera)

These will calculate F values with picture and camera as random effects for which to compare fixed effects, camera and individual, respectively.  This overrides using digitization as the error for each effect, which would be incorrect in a nested ANOVA framework.

You could also trick our bilat.symmerty function if you wanted with 

bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, side = camera, rep = picture, object.sym = FALSE, …)

The ANOVA would be set up correctly but have the terms ind, side, and rep instead of your variable names.  This function is designed to deal with paired shapes, which you kind of have with the cameras.  The object.sym = FALSE is to make sure the analysis knows that there are separate landmark configurations (matching symmetry) rather than left and right halves of the same configuration.  

The two approaches should give you similar results although the ANOVA tables will be constructed slightly different.  (The former considers camera to be a fixed effect with respect to digitization; the latter uses a three-way interaction and keeps camera as a random effect.)

Hope that helps!
Mike

Hi Richie,

Unless you a have specific type of digitization process that is used for digitization 1 and another for digitization 2, there really is no interaction to measure.  I understood your initial explanation as you digitize twice so that you can have a handle on measurement error (via digitizing).  You could add + picture:digitization to your formula, but it should result in no error.

You can call it error or call it picture:digitization and it will be the same thing, unless there are different factor levels, 1 and 2, within digitization that mean something.

Mike

parts:
Richie,

 

Let me chime in here.  I think there was a piece of what Mike stated that was missed from a statistical perspective. What Mike was saying is that from the description of your nested design and digitization, there IS no additional variation that could be explained by any possible interaction term. Think of it this way.  You digitized each picture twice. Thus, if you obtain SSCamera, and then SSPicture and then SSDig, there is no variation left to explain.  All sums-of-squares are perfectly described in this case by these components; there is nothing left. For this reason, the nested design would test SSPicture against SSDig (with SSDig serving as the EMS error), then SSCamera is tested against SSPicture, with SSPicture serving as its EMS.

 

Perhaps it is instructive to think of a simple univariate case to recall what is meant by a nested model in terms of the sums of squares. Think of 2 factors, A and B.  A full factorial design has SSA, SSB, and SSA:B; the last of which is the interaction term. With a nested model we have SSA and SSB nested within A: there is no interaction.  But look deeper: if one looks at the nested SS we find that the SS for the nested term (call it SSB(A)) actually equals the sum of SSB and SSA:B from the factorial design. In other words, the nested term describes all of the SS for factor B, as well as its interaction with A (code below).  This is why with the design you described there is no additional interaction. The simple example below shows mathematically how this is in fact the case.

 

Hope this helps,


Dean

 

y<-rnorm(30)

x<-gl(2,15)

x2<-gl(2,1,30)

 

anova(lm(y~x*x2))

anova(lm(y~x/x2))

 

Dean

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA with nested measurement error
parts:
Dean,

Oh I see! so if a factor is nested in another factor, what might appear to be a main effect of the nested factor in the output also includes interactions with the factors it's nested in?

So how do we parse these effects? What i'd really need is to know if digitising error is different for different camera types. Perhaps I could program up a permutation test where i resample the procrustes distance between digitisations for camera 1 and 2. problem is this as i have 4 digitisations from the same person per camera there would be non-independence of data points, and so maybe i should just randomly pic 1 picture from each person and each camera and use them? i'd lose half my observations but 344 should be fine i guess.

Let me know what you think.

Richie
On Tuesday, October 17, 2017 at 9:02:06 PM UTC+1, Dean Adams wrote:

Richie,

 

Let me chime in here.  I think there was a piece of what Mike stated that was missed from a statistical perspective. What Mike was saying is that from the description of your nested design and digitization, there IS no additional variation that could be explained by any possible interaction term. Think of it this way.  You digitized each picture twice. Thus, if you obtain SSCamera, and then SSPicture and then SSDig, there is no variation left to explain.  All sums-of-squares are perfectly described in this case by these components; there is nothing left. For this reason, the nested design would test SSPicture against SSDig (with SSDig serving as the EMS error), then SSCamera is tested against SSPicture, with SSPicture serving as its EMS.

 

Perhaps it is instructive to think of a simple univariate case to recall what is meant by a nested model in terms of the sums of squares. Think of 2 factors, A and B.  A full factorial design has SSA, SSB, and SSA:B; the last of which is the interaction term. With a nested model we have SSA and SSB nested within A: there is no interaction.  But look deeper: if one looks at the nested SS we find that the SS for the nested term (call it SSB(A)) actually equals the sum of SSB and SSA:B from the factorial design. In other words, the nested term describes all of the SS for factor B, as well as its interaction with A (code below).  This is why with the design you described there is no additional interaction. The simple example below shows mathematically how this is in fact the case.

 

Hope this helps,


Dean

 

y<-rnorm(30)

x<-gl(2,15)

x2<-gl(2,1,30)

 

anova(lm(y~x*x2))

anova(lm(y~x/x2))

 

Dean

Unless you a have specific type of digitization process that is used for digitization 1 and another for digitization 2, there really is no interaction to measure.  I understood your initial explanation as you digitize twice so that you can have a handle on measurement error (via digitizing).  You could add + picture:digitization to your formula, but it should result in no error.

On Tuesday, October 17, 2017 at 3:21:51 PM UTC+1, Michael Collyer wrote:

Hi Richie,

 

You will forgive me for answering with a bias toward our functions, but that is the easiest way for me to approach this.

 

Once you have performed GPA and acquired your Procrustes residuals, call this array, “shape”, you probably want to do an analysis like this:

 

fit <- procD.lm(shape ~ ind/camera + camera/picture, ...)

 

Note that “digitization” is not needed as a variable, as it is the error term for picture.  This formula includes ind:camera and camera:picture interactions, but does not assume all levels of one are represented with all levels of the other, in case that is an issue.  (It also does not force the random effect to be represented as a fixed effect in the model.)

 

For evaluation, you will want to also do this:

 

fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ camera/picture)

fit <- nested.update(fit, ~ ind/camera)

 

These will calculate F values with picture and camera as random effects for which to compare fixed effects, camera and individual, respectively.  This overrides using digitization as the error for each effect, which would be incorrect in a nested ANOVA framework.

 

You could also trick our bilat.symmerty function if you wanted with 

 

bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, side = camera, rep = picture, object.sym = FALSE, …)

 

The ANOVA would be set up correctly but have the terms ind, side, and rep instead of your variable names.  This function is designed to deal with paired shapes, which you kind of have with the cameras.  The object.sym = FALSE is to make sure the analysis knows that there are separate landmark configurations (matching symmetry) rather than left and right halves of the same configuration.  

 

The two approaches should give you similar results although the ANOVA tables will be constructed slightly different.  (The former considers camera to be a fixed effect with respect to digitization; the latter uses a three-way interaction and keeps camera as a random effect.)

 

Hope that helps!

Mike
On Oct 17, 2017, at 4:54 AM, Thomas Richardson <thomasricha...@outlook.com> wrote:

all,

 

So I'm struggling to work out how to write the formula for my Procrustes ANOVA in R. I have photographs of 86 human faces, where i took 2 photos each with 2 cameras (4 photos each) and digitised each face twice. I do this because i suspect one camera is more distorted to the other and want to model this distortion, as well as how it possibly interacts with other variables (e.g. fluctuating and directional asymmetry) and sources of measurement error. having 2 digitisations per picture allows me to estimate digitisation error, and 2 pictures allow me to estimate error associated with any 2 pictures (taken 1 minute apart).

 

 

 

 

So my data is completely nested: digitisations nested in pictures which are nested in camera-type which is nested in individuals. How would i represent this in a procrustes anova formula? I've heard that it's represented as an interaction effect, such that the main effect of digitsation error would be:

 

individual*camera*picture*digitsation


? 

 

This terminology would be a problem if i wanted to see if different cameras produce different levels of digitisation error, which I do, as this would be an interaction between the term above and camera, so:

 

individual*camera*picture*digitisation:camera


Which really doesn't look right.

 

Really what im trying to get is the main effect of each of my sources of measurement error, as well as 2 way interactions between them and camera type 

 

Can anyone help me out?

 

Thanks

 

Richie

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Procrustes ANOVA with nested measurement error
parts:
One way is to treat this as a factorial design rather than a nested one. In that case one has main effects and interaction terms, and the camera:digitization term would be the component you are interested in I believe. If significant it implies that the variation across digitizing runs differs based on the camera type. I post hoc test (of disparity not means) would then allow you to determine which camera displayed greater variation across digitizing runs; which would in effect be greater error.


Bear in mind though that the latter step must be done carefully so as not to conflate variation across pictures with variation across digitizing runs.  

 

D
